Thin-Film Encapsulations: Compared to standard glass encapsulations, thin-film encapsulations aim to reduce weight and improve flexibility. Al O and SiO are common 2 3 2 material systems used in thin-film encapsulations due to their impermeability to oxygen and water.64–67 Nevertheless, a single Al O or SiO thin-film typically offers only one to 2 3 2 three orders of magnitude reduction in water vapor transmission rates (WVTR)46 due to the tendency of inorganic materials to form and propagate diffusion pathways (e.g., pores and pinholes). Although optimized atomic layer deposited (ALD) single-layer systems reach below 10-3 g/m2/day,68–70 defect passivation methods remain a challenge for further reduction using inorganic systems alone. Advanced multilayer systems implementing polymer-based passivation techniques, particularly inorganic/organic multilayered systems (Figure 2), have been identified as an effective method for reducing permeability while maintaining optical transparency71,72 and mechanical flexibility.73,74 In effect, the polymer interlayer decouples defects in the inorganic layers to create long tortuous diffusion pathways through the multilayer stack.54,75 This established method can reduce WVTRs to nearly 10-6 g/m2/day, as demonstrated by commercially available Ultra-High Barrier films from 3M,76 and BarixTM from Vitex Systems.77 Figure 2: Concept image of an inorganic/organic multilayer system with 5.5 dyads. Transparent Conductive Gas Diffusion Barriers: Beyond weight reduction and improved mechanical flexibility, thin-films can provide yet another functionality: electrical conductivity. In the following section, we discuss encapsulations composed of metals and metal oxides, which serve as both transparent conductors and gas diffusion barriers. 5/52 DE-EE0010241 Nicolas Gaillard Single-layer thin film barriers: Transparent conductive oxides (TCO) are indispensable in optoelectronic devices due to their high transparencies and electrical conductivities. However, for TCOs to function as a gas diffusion barrier, it’s important to reduce the size and number of defect-driven permeation pathways (e.g., pores, pinholes, grain boundaries).49,51–54 In all practicality, typical thin-film TCOs prepared using conventional deposition techniques (i.e., sputtering, evaporation) will have defects (Figure 3a) and offer only one to two orders of magnitude improvement in WVTRs (Table 1). As such, advanced deposition techniques (e.g., doped ALD) have been at the forefront of single- layer TCGDB optimization, which results in amorphous high-density structures with low WVTRs (Figure 3b).78 Despite the remarkable result, the electrical conductivity and barrier properties of TCOs can degrade under damp heat conditions and require robust material systems to mitigate this issue.18,78 In addition to environmental deterioration, brittle oxide films on ductile substrates can result in the deterioration of electrical properties under a moderate amount of strain (approx. 1-3%),79–82 similar to SiO ,83 and Al O ,84 which 2 2 3 demonstrates mechanical flexibility only up to 1-2% strain. Overall, single-layer TCO barrier systems are inherently riddled with sub-micrometer intergranular defects and grain boundaries, which act as permeation pathways.46,47 As such, optimization of TCO microstructures by ALD and intermittent doping is required to improve barrier performance.
